title: The Red Shoes

full_text:
There was once a pretty, delicate peasant girl named Karen who was so poor that she had to go barefoot in summer, and in winter wore heavy wooden clogs that made her ankles red and sore.

An old shoemaker's wife made Karen a pair of shoes from scraps of red cloth. They were clumsy, but Karen thought them the most wonderful things in the world.

When Karen's mother died, an elderly lady took pity on the child, took her into her home, and gave her clean clothes. Karen grew into lovely maidenhood, but vanity began to fester in her heart.

On the day of her confirmation in the great church, Karen deceived the half-blind old lady and bought a pair of dazzling red morocco leather dancing shoes meant for a countess. Throughout the solemn service, while the bishop placed his hands upon her head, Karen thought of nothing but her red shoes, admiring their glossy shine upon the flagstones.

When the old lady fell critically ill, Karen neglected her nursing duties to attend a grand midnight ball in town. The moment Karen stepped onto the ballroom floor, the red shoes took complete control of her feet!

They danced her out through the palace doors, down the marble steps, and into the dark streets. Karen tried to stop, but the shoes were glued to her feet; she tried to turn left, but the shoes danced right. Out into the dark forest they whirled her, through thorns and briars that tore her skin, past the executioner's hut where an angel with a flaming sword blocked her path: "Thou shalt dance in thy pride until thy skin shrivels to bone!"

Weeping in agony, Karen danced through day and night, through rain and snow, unable to rest or sleep. Driven to utter despair, she danced to the executioner's cottage and begged: "Chop off my feet with your axe, for I can endure this torment no longer!"

The executioner severed the shoes with his blade; and lo! The severed red shoes, with little feet inside, danced away into the forest depths and vanished.

The executioner carved her two wooden crutches, and Karen devoted the rest of her life to humble labor and heartfelt prayers in the village church. When her soul was purified of all vanity, an angel appeared in the nave, touched her with a green branch, and carried her forgiven spirit into the eternal mercy of heaven.
moral: Obsessive vanity leads the soul into uncontrollable torment; humble repentance alone restores peace.

quiz.question: What fundamental virtue is highlighted in "The Red Shoes"?
options: Andersen's tales teach compassion, resilience, and Christian hope
Acting in hasty anger without listening

By shouting loudly and blaming friends

options: Patience, honesty, and humility lead to lasting harmony
